Volcanoes

Educational information. Individual clinical review of this presentation by Dr. Ehsan is not yet documented. It does not replace personal medical evaluation.

Source: MedlinePlus, National Library of Medicine. Read the original source

MedlinePlus data edition September 26, 2026. Imported September 27, 2026. These dates do not indicate a new clinical review of the article.

A volcano is a vent in the Earth's crust. Hot rock, steam, poisonous gases, and ash reach the Earth's surface when a volcano erupts. An eruption can also cause earthquakes, mudflows and flash floods, rock falls and landslides, acid rain, fires, and even tsunamis.

Volcanic gas and ash can damage the lungs of small infants, older adults, and people with severe respiratory illnesses. Volcanic ash can affect people hundreds of miles away from the eruption.

Although there are no guarantees of safety during a volcanic eruption, you can take actions to protect yourself. You should have a disaster plan. Being prepared can help reduce fear, anxiety, and losses. If you do experience a disaster, it is normal to feel stressed. You may need help in finding ways to cope.

Questions for your care team

General prompts to help prepare for your appointment.

  • How does this information apply to my situation?
  • Which symptoms or results need evaluation?
  • Which tests are useful, and what can they tell us?
  • What care options, benefits, and risks should we discuss?
  • When should I seek urgent help, and whom should I call?
  • When is follow-up, and how will we know whether the plan is working?

For a life-threatening emergency, call 911 in the U.S. or your local emergency number.
